claim: Members of the SLC26 family constitute a conserved class of anion transport proteins, which encompasses uncoupled transporters with channel-like properties, coupled exchangers and motor proteins.
source: Members of the SLC26 family constitute a conserved class of anion transport proteins, which encompasses uncoupled transporters with channel-like properties, coupled exchangers and motor proteins.
evidence: This is a general characterization of the SLC26 family based on established scientific knowledge and literature.

claim: Among the 10 functional paralogs in humans, several participate in the secretion of bicarbonate in exchange with chloride and thus play an important role in maintaining pH homeostasis.
source: Among the 10 functional paralogs in humans, several participate in the secretion of bicarbonate in exchange with chloride and thus play an important role in maintaining pH homeostasis.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about human SLC26 paralogs and their physiological roles.

claim: The structure of murine SLC26A9 has been elucidated and its function defined as an uncoupled chloride transporter.
source: Previously, we have elucidated the structure of murine SLC26A9 and defined its function as an uncoupled chloride transporter (Walter et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The structure of human transporter SLC26A6 has been determined.
source: Here we have determined the structure of the closely related human transporter SLC26A6 and characterized it as a coupled exchanger of chloride with bicarbonate and presumably also oxalate.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by cryo-EM data presented in the results.

claim: SLC26A6 is characterized as a coupled exchanger of chloride with bicarbonate and presumably also oxalate.
source: Here we have determined the structure of the closely related human transporter SLC26A6 and characterized it as a coupled exchanger of chloride with bicarbonate and presumably also oxalate.
evidence: This characterization is supported by functional assays presented in Figure 1.

claim: The structure of SLC26A6 defines an inward-facing conformation of the protein that generally resembles known structures of SLC26A9.
source: The structure defines an inward-facing conformation of the protein that generally resembles known structures of SLC26A9.
evidence: This is supported by structural data and comparison shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The altered anion selectivity between SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 is a consequence of a remodeled ion binding site located in the center of a mobile unit of the membrane-inserted domain.
source: The altered anion selectivity between both paralogs is a consequence of a remodeled ion binding site located in the center of a mobile unit of the membrane-inserted domain, which also accounts for differences in the coupling mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and mutagenesis data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Bicarbonate is a waste product of the citric acid cycle and an important buffer in the intra- and extracellular environment.
source: Bicarbonate (HCO3-), the conjugate base of carbonic acid, is a waste product of the citric acid cycle and an important buffer in the intra- and extracellular environment.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Transport of bicarbonate across cellular membranes constitutes an important mechanism for the control of intracellular pH and the increase of the buffer capacity of bodily fluids and secretions.
source: Its transport across cellular membranes thus constitutes an important mechanism for the control of intracellular pH and the increase of the buffer capacity of bodily fluids and secretions (Alka and Casey, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Bicarbonate transport is mediated by distinct channels and secondary transporters, including paralogs of the SLC4 and SLC26 families.
source: This process is mediated by distinct channels and secondary transporters, the latter comprising paralogs of the SLC4 and SLC26 families.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bicarbonate transport mechanisms.

claim: The SLC26 transporters constitute an abundant class of anion transport proteins that are expressed in all kingdoms of life with a considerable degree of sequence conservation.
source: The SLC26 transporters constitute an abundant class of anion transport proteins that are expressed in all kingdoms of life with a considerable degree of sequence conservation (Alper and Sharma, 2013; Dorwart et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Homologs of SLC26 in prokaryotes and plants were classified as symporters, where the uptake of mono- and divalent anions is coupled to the import of either sodium ions or protons.
source: Homologs in prokaryotes and plants were classified as symporters, where the uptake of mono- and divalent anions is coupled to the import of either sodium ions or protons (Geertsma et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SLC26 transporters in animals show mechanistic differences compared to prokaryotic and plant homologs.
source: However, the transporters in animals show mechanistic differences.
evidence: This is inferred from the context and supported by the subsequent description of functional diversity.

claim: Among the 10 functional SLC26 paralogs in humans, there is an astonishing mechanistic breadth.
source: Among the 10 functional SLC26 paralogs in humans, we find an astonishing mechanistic breadth.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about the functional diversity of human SLC26 paralogs.

claim: SLC26 family members function as either coupled anion exchangers, anion transporters with channel-like properties, or as a motor protein in the case of SLC26A5 (Prestin).
source: Family members function as either coupled anion exchangers, anion transporters with channel-like properties and in the case of SLC26A5 (Prestin), as a motor protein in cochlear outer hair cells (Alper and Sharma, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The distinction between coupled and uncoupled transporters is most pronounced among the SLC26 paralogs which have retained their transport function.
source: Among the paralogs which have retained their transport function, the distinction between coupled and uncoupled transporters is most pronounced.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional characterization of family members.

claim: Most SLC26 family members operate as exchangers of different anions including chloride, bicarbonate, iodide, formate, sulfate, and oxalate.
source: Whereas most family members operate as exchangers of different anions including the monovalent ions chloride (Cl-), HCO3-, iodide (I-) and formate and the divalent ions sulfate and oxalate (Alper and Sharma, 2013), the protein SLC26A9 functions as fast passive transporter of Cl- (Dorwart et al., 2007; Walter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SLC26A9 functions as a fast passive transporter of chloride.
source: Whereas most family members operate as exchangers of different anions including the monovalent ions chloride (Cl-), HCO3-, iodide (I-) and formate and the divalent ions sulfate and oxalate (Alper and Sharma, 2013), the protein SLC26A9 functions as fast passive transporter of Cl- (Dorwart et al., 2007; Walter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The murine ortholog of SLC26A9 adopts a homodimeric architecture that is representative for the entire SLC26 family.
source: The protein adopts a homodimeric architecture that is representative for the entire SLC26 family.
evidence: This is supported by prior structural work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Each subunit of SLC26A9 consists of a membrane-inserted transport domain (TM) followed by a cytoplasmic STAS domain.
source: Each subunit consists of a membrane-inserted transport domain (TM) followed by a cytoplasmic STAS domain, which together with the extended N-terminus mediates the bulk of the subunit interactions with few contacts in the membrane-inserted region (Walter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: The TMs of SLC26 family members share a protein fold that was initially identified in the prokaryotic transporter UraA.
source: The TMs share a protein fold that was initially identified in the prokaryotic transporter UraA (Lu et al., 2011), and that was later defined in the prokaryotic homologue SLC26Dg as common architecture for the entire family (Geertsma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: In the SLC26 architecture, the TM segregates into two separate motifs termed 'core' and 'gate' domains that adopt distinct roles during transport.
source: In this architecture, the TM segregates into two separate motifs that adopt distinct roles during transport, respectively termed 'core' and 'gate' domains.
evidence: This is supported by prior structural characterization of SLC26 family members.

claim: The gate domain forms a contiguous rigid scaffold with the cytosolic STAS domain that remains static during transport.
source: The gate domain forms a contiguous rigid scaffold with the cytosolic STAS domain that remains static during transport.
evidence: This is supported by prior structural and functional studies.

claim: The mobile core domain harbors a selective anion binding site and acts as mobile unit during transport.
source: Conversely the mobile core domain harbors a selective anion binding site and acts as mobile unit during transport.
evidence: This is supported by prior structural and functional studies.

claim: The core domain alternately exposes the substrate site to different sides of the membrane as expected for a protein working by an elevator-type transport mechanism.
source: This unit alternately exposes the substrate site to different sides of the membrane as expected for a protein working by an elevator-type transport mechanism (Drew and Boudker, 2016; Walter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on elevator-type mechanisms.

claim: SLC26A9 mediates large channel-like chloride currents that saturate at high mM concentration.
source: Despite its classification as membrane transporter, SLC26A9 mediates large channel-like chloride currents that saturate at high mM concentration and it efficiently discriminates against HCO3- (Dorwart et al., 2007; Walter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior functional studies.

claim: SLC26A9 efficiently discriminates against bicarbonate.
source: Despite its classification as membrane transporter, SLC26A9 mediates large channel-like chloride currents that saturate at high mM concentration and it efficiently discriminates against HCO3- (Dorwart et al., 2007; Walter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior functional studies.

claim: SLC26A9's function as a fast electrogenic chloride transporter and selection against bicarbonate is astonishing since several other family members have been classified as Cl-/HCO3- exchangers.
source: Its function as a fast electrogenic chloride transporter and selection against HCO3- is astonishing since several other family members have been classified as Cl-/ HCO3- exchangers (Alper and Sharma, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with other family members, supported by citation.

claim: SLC26A6 has been classified as a Cl-/HCO3- exchanger.
source: One of the family members sharing this property is the protein SLC26A6 (Knauf et al., 2001; Lohi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SLC26A6 is widely expressed in different tissues including the heart, kidney, pancreas, and intestine.
source: SLC26A6 is widely expressed in different tissues including the heart, kidney, pancreas, and intestine (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: SLC26A6 plays an important role in the extrusion of oxalate to prevent the formation of kidney stones.
source: Besides its function as a HCO3- transporter, it also plays an important role in the extrusion of oxalate to prevent the formation of kidney stones (Clark et al., 2008; Jiang et al., 2006; Ohana et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SLC26A6 acts in synergy with the chloride channel CFTR and was proposed to engage in direct interaction and mutual regulation.
source: Similar to SLC26A9, the protein acts in synergy with the chloride channel CFTR and was proposed to engage in direct interaction and mutual regulation (Bertrand et al., 2017; Dorwart et al., 2008; Shcheynikov et al., 2006a; Wang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The stoichiometry of HCO3- and oxalate transport by SLC26A6 is controversial, as transport of both ions has been described in different studies as either electrogenic or electroneutral.
source: The stoichiometry of HCO3- and oxalate transport by SLC26 is still controversial, as transport of both ions has been described in different studies as either electrogenic or electroneutral (Chernova et al., 2005; Clark et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2013; Ohana et al., 2009; Shcheynikov et al., 2006b; Xie et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies with conflicting results.

claim: The structural basis for the mechanistic distinction between the uncoupled SLC26A9 and the coupled SLC26A6 and the basis for their pronounced selectivity has remained elusive.
source: Consequently, the structural basis for the mechanistic distinction between the uncoupled SLC26A9 and the coupled SLC26A6 and the basis for their pronounced selectivity, with Cl- acting as common substrate of both proteins, has remained elusive.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: Murine SLC26A9 mediates comparatively large and selective Cl- currents.
source: We have previously characterized the transport properties of murine SLC26A9 by patch clamp electrophysiology and found comparatively large and selective Cl- currents.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and prior work.

claim: SLC26A9 currents reverse at the Nernst potential of the conducting anion, which distinguishes the protein as an uncoupled chloride transporter.
source: SLC26A9 currents were shown to reverse at the Nernst potential of the conducting anion, which distinguishes the protein as an uncoupled chloride transporter (Walter et al., 2019; Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and citation to prior work.

claim: The high magnitude of SLC26A9 ohmic currents, which lack any time-dependence in response to voltage changes, originate from an unusually active protein that transports anions with channel-like properties.
source: The high magnitude of these ohmic currents, which lack any time-dependence in response to voltage changes, originate from an unusually active protein that transports anions with channel-like properties (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SLC26A9 shows a lyotropic permeability sequence that facilitates the transport of Cl-, isothiocyanate, I- and nitrate but not sulfate or HCO3-.
source: SLC26A9 shows a lyotropic permeability sequence that facilitates the transport of Cl-, isothiocyanate, I- and nitrate but not sulfate or HCO3- (Walter et al., 2019; Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The inability of SLC26A9 to conduct HCO3- is an exception in a family where most members work as transporters of this abundant anion.
source: The inability to conduct HCO3- is an exception in a family where most members work as transporters of this abundant anion (Alper and Sharma, 2013; Ohana et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: No specific currents could be attributed to SLC26A6 in patch clamp electrophysiology in a wide voltage range, irrespective of whether symmetric Cl- solutions or asymmetric conditions with extracellular HCO3- were used.
source: However, unlike for SLC26A9, we did not detect specific currents that could be attributed to SLC26A6 in a wide voltage range. This was irrespective of whether we used symmetric Cl- solutions or asymmetric conditions, where the major anion in the extracellular solution was changed to HCO3- (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Surface biotinylation confirmed expression of SLC26A6 at the plasma membrane at a similar level as observed for SLC26A9.
source: To confirm the expression of SLC26A6 at the plasma membrane, we employed surface biotinylation and found a similar level as observed for its electrogenic paralog SLC26A9 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The lack of detectable currents for SLC26A6 suggests that the transporter would either be inactive, exceedingly slow or that transport would be electroneutral as a consequence of the strict 1:1 exchange of two monovalent anions.
source: We thus concluded that the transporter would either be inactive, exceedingly slow or that transport would be electroneutral as a consequence of the strict 1:1 exchange of two monovalent anions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiology results.

claim: No acidification was observed for SLC26A6 in the ACMA assay, in contrast to SLC26A9.
source: However, in contrast to SLC26A9, no acidification was observed for SLC26A6, emphasizing that the transporter is either inactive or, alternatively, transport would be strictly coupled and electroneutral (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SLC26A6 mediates a robust time-dependent fluorescence decrease at high Cl- concentration in the lucigenin assay, demonstrating Cl- transport.
source: In this assay, we found a robust time-dependent fluorescence decrease at high Cl- concentration, demonstrating its transport by SLC26A6 (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Cl- transport by SLC26A6 did not require the addition of valinomycin to dissipate the membrane potential, underlining that transport is electroneutral.
source: The process did not require the addition of valinomycin to dissipate the membrane potential, thus underlining that transport is electroneutral.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation that valinomycin was not needed.

claim: The Cl- concentration-dependence of transport by SLC26A6 showed saturation with an apparent KM of about 16–37 mM.
source: In the investigation of the Cl- concentration-dependence of transport, we found a saturation with an apparent KM of about 16–37 mM (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The low affinity for Cl- in SLC26A6 is in the same range as observed for Cl- transport in SLC26A9.
source: This indicated low affinity for the transported anion is in the same range as observed for Cl- transport in SLC26A9 (Walter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison based on data from the current study and prior work.

claim: The addition of 10 mM HCO3- to the outside of proteoliposomes containing SLC26A6 in presence of symmetric 200 mM Cl- caused a pronounced increase in luminescence of the HCO3--selective europium probe.
source: The addition of 10 mM HCO3- to the outside in presence of a symmetric 200 mM concentration of Cl- on both sides of the membrane caused a pronounced increase in luminescence that is well above the small non-specific signal observed in liposomes not containing any protein (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The luminescence increase from HCO3- influx is substantially enhanced when using a reduced outside Cl- concentration of 50 mM to generate an outwardly directed driving force.
source: This increase is substantially enhanced when using a reduced outside Cl- concentration of 50 mM to generate an outwardly directed driving force (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The experiments demonstrate that HCO3- is a transported anion and that its import into proteoliposomes is coupled to the counterflow of Cl-.
source: Together these experiments demonstrate that HCO3- is a transported anion and that its import into proteoliposomes is coupled to the counterflow of Cl-.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results from the lucigenin and europium probe assays.

claim: SLC26A6 was proposed to be involved in the transport of oxalate in exchange for Cl- and thus to participate in the excretion of this small divalent anion in both the intestine and kidneys.
source: Besides HCO3-, SLC26A6 was also proposed to be involved in the transport of oxalate in exchange for Cl- and thus to participate in the excretion of this small divalent anion in both the intestine and kidneys (Clark et al., 2008; Ohana et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: If assuming a coupled 1:1 stoichiometry for Cl-/oxalate exchange, the transported charge would no longer be balanced, thus converting an electroneutral into an electrogenic transport process.
source: However, if assuming a coupled 1:1 stoichiometry as observed in case of Cl-/HCO3- exchange, the transported charge would in this case no longer be balanced, thus converting an electroneutral into an electrogenic transport process.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the charge states of the ions.

claim: A robust decrease of the ACMA fluorescence was found upon the addition of extracellular oxalate to Cl--loaded proteoliposomes containing SLC26A6.
source: In these experiments, we found a robust decrease of the ACMA fluorescence upon the addition of extracellular oxalate to Cl--loaded proteoliposomes containing SLC26A6, with the concentration dependence and saturation of the fluorescence decay further emphasizing a specific transport process (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Electrogenic Cl-/oxalate exchange by SLC26A6 could not be detected by patch clamp electrophysiology in the whole cell configuration, likely due to the slow kinetics of the process.
source: We also attempted to follow electrogenic Cl-/oxalate exchange by patch clamp electrophysiology in the whole cell configuration but did not measure pronounced currents that would be above background, likely due to the slow kinetics of the process (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and inference about kinetics.

claim: The functional experiments characterize SLC26A6 as a strictly coupled transporter that exchanges Cl- with HCO3- and presumably also oxalate at a 1:1 stoichiometric ratio.
source: Together, our functional experiments characterize SLC26A6 as a strictly coupled transporter that exchanges Cl- with HCO3- and presumably also oxalate at a 1:1 stoichiometric ratio.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The structure of SLC26A6 was determined by cryo-electron microscopy at 3.3 Å resolution.
source: A dataset of the protein purified in the detergent glycol-diosgenin (GDN) at 3.3 Å was of high quality and allowed for the unambiguous interpretation of the cryo-EM density by an atomic model (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2,Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The SLC26A6 structure shows familiar features that have previously been observed in various eukaryotic family members including human and murine SLC26A9, SLC26A5, SLC26A4, and the plant transporter AtSULTR4.
source: In its organization, the SLC26A6 structure shows familiar features that have previously been observed in various eukaryotic family members of known structure including human and murine SLC26A9 (Chi et al., 2020; Walter et al., 2019), SLC26A5 (Bavi et al., 2021; Butan et al., 2022; Futamata et al., 2022; Ge et al., 2021), SLC26A4 (Liu et al., 2023) and the plant transporter AtSULTR4 (Wang et al., 2021; Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with prior structures cited in the text.

claim: The SLC26A6 subunit consists of a membrane-inserted unit (TM) followed by a cytoplasmic STAS domain.
source: The SLC26A6 subunit consists of a membrane-inserted unit (TM) followed by a cytoplasmic STAS domain.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the homodimeric SLC26A6 protein, subunit interactions are predominantly formed by the domain-swapped cytoplasmic parts including an extended N-terminal region and the C-terminal STAS domain.
source: In the homodimeric protein, subunit interactions are predominantly formed by the domain-swapped cytoplasmic parts including an extended N-terminal region and the C-terminal STAS domain, whereas the few contacts between the transmembrane transport units are confined to the end of the terminal membrane-spanning helix α14 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A region connecting secondary structure elements of the STAS domain (located between Cα1 and β4) termed the intervening sequence (IVS) is present in SLC26A6.
source: A region connecting secondary structure elements of the STAS domain (located between Cα1 and β4) termed the intervening sequence (IVS) is present in the characterized protein (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Removal of the IVS region increased both the stability and surface expression of a construct of the murine SLC26A9 while retaining its transport properties.
source: Previously, removal of this region increased both the stability and surface expression of a construct of the murine SLC26A9 while retaining its transport properties (Walter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the SLC26A6 structure, the N-terminal part of the IVS folds into an α-helix encompassing amino acids 569–593 (CαIVS) whereas the following 61 residues are unstructured and thus not resolved in the density.
source: In the density, the N-terminal part of the IVS folds into an α-helix encompassing amino acids 569–593 (CαIVS) whereas the following 61 residues are unstructured and thus not resolved in the density (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: On the C-terminus of the IVS, the density re-appears at Ser 655 at the region preceding β4, which interacts with CαIVS.
source: On the C-terminus of the IVS, the density re-appears at Ser 655 at the region preceding β4, which interacts with CαIVS (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: A generally similar arrangement of the IVS was also observed in a full-length construct of human SLC26A9.
source: A generally similar arrangement was also observed in a full-length construct of human SLC26A9 (Chi et al., 2020; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and comparison shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In both SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 structures, CαIVS runs about parallel to the membrane plane and contacts the loop connecting α8 and α9 of the mobile core domain.
source: In both structures, CαIVS runs about parallel to the membrane plane and contacts the loop connecting α8 and α9 of the mobile core domain.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: The interaction between CαIVS and the core domain loop presumably influences the conformational preferences of the core domain thereby potentially impacting transport.
source: This presumably influences its conformational preferences thereby potentially impacting transport (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observation.

claim: In the dimeric SLC26A6 transporter, the two TMs share minimal contacts and thus supposedly function as independent units.
source: In the dimeric transporter, the two TMs share minimal contacts and thus supposedly function as independent units (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Structural differences underlying the distinct transport properties of SLC26 paralogs are expected to be manifested in the TM part of the protein.
source: Consequently, we expect structural differences underlying the distinct transport properties of SLC26 paralogs to be manifested in this part of the protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural organization.

claim: The TMs of SLC26A6 consist of two topologically related repeats of seven transmembrane segments, which span the membrane with opposite orientation.
source: Like in other pro- and eukaryotic family members of known structure, the TMs of SLC26A6 consist of two topologically related repeats of seven transmembrane segments, which span the membrane with opposite orientation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Elements of both repeats in the TM are intertwined to form two segregated modules, a gate domain and a core domain.
source: Elements of both repeats are intertwined to form two segregated modules, a gate domain and a core domain (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The TMs of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 superimpose with an RMSD of 1.3 Å, illustrating their equivalence.
source: The equivalence between the SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 conformations is illustrated in the overlay of the respective TMs whose Cα positions superimpose with an RMSD of 1.3 Å (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 conformations represent inward-facing states of transporters presumably functioning by an alternate access mechanism.
source: Both conformations represent inward-facing states of transporters presumably functioning by an alternate access mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and knowledge of transporter mechanisms.

claim: The substrate binding site located in the center of the core domain is accessible from the cytoplasm via a spacious aqueous cavity, whereas the extracellular exit is sealed by extended contacts between core and gate domains.
source: The substrate binding site located in the center of the core domain is accessible from the cytoplasm via a spacious aqueous cavity, whereas the extracellular exit is sealed by extended contacts between core and gate domains (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3C, D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The resemblance between individual sub-domains of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 exceeds the overall similarity of the TM, with core- and gate domains superimposing with RMSDs of 1.13 Å and 1.2 Å, respectively.
source: The resemblance between individual sub-domains even exceeds the overall similarity of the TM (with core- and gate domains superimposing with RMSDs of 1.13 Å and 1.2 Å, respectively) distinguishing them as largely independent units of a modular protein (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The gate domains of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 do not show pronounced differences.
source: In the comparison of both paralogs, the gate domains do not show pronounced differences (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The gate domains together with the cytoplasmic STAS domains form a contiguous rigid scaffold of the dimeric protein that presumably remains static during transport.
source: Together with the cytoplasmic STAS domains, which constitute the bulk of the dimer interface, these sub-domains form a contiguous rigid scaffold of the dimeric protein that presumably remains static during transport (Figure 2B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both core domains represent the mobile elements of the protein.
source: In contrast, both core domains represent the mobile elements of the protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and knowledge of transporter mechanisms.

claim: Each core domain carries a substrate binding site located in a pocket at the center of the unit facing the gate domain.
source: Each core domain carries a substrate binding site located in a pocket at the center of the unit facing the gate domain (Figures 3C, D ,, 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figures 3C, D and 4A.

claim: The presumable location of a bound chloride ion is resolved in the structure of SLC26A6 at a low contour of the map.
source: The presumable location of a bound chloride ion is resolved in the structure of SLC26A6 at a low contour of the map (Figure 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The position of the bound chloride in SLC26A6 concurs with positions inferred from known structures of paralogs, which show binding of Cl- and HCO3- to an equivalent location.
source: This position concurs with positions inferred from known structures of paralogs, which show binding of Cl- and HCO3- to an equivalent location (Chi et al., 2020; Futamata et al., 2022; Ge et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023; Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with prior structures cited in the text.

claim: The anion binding site is placed between the opposed short helices α3 and α10, which partly span the membrane and whose N-termini are aligned to face each other in the center of the core domain.
source: The anion binding site is placed between the opposed short helices α3 and α10, which partly span the membrane and whose N-termini are aligned to face each other in the center of the core domain (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Together with the side chains of surrounding residues, both α-helix termini form a selective anion binding site.
source: Together with the side chains of surrounding residues, both α-helix termini form a selective anion binding site (Figure 4B–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4B–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In complex with its bound cargo, the core domain is believed to shuttle as rigid unit between two extreme conformations where the binding site is either exposed to the cytoplasm or the extracellular environment.
source: In complex with its bound cargo, the core domain is believed to shuttle as rigid unit between two extreme conformations where the binding site is either exposed to the cytoplasm or the extracellular environment (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and knowledge of elevator-type transport mechanisms.

claim: The core domains presumably display the characteristic features accounting for the distinct functional properties of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9.
source: As carrier of the substrate binding site, the core domains presumably display the characteristic features accounting for the distinct functional properties of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and functional differences.

claim: The conservation of core domains within the SLC26 family is illustrated in the comparison of the respective domains of SLC26A6 and SLC26A5 (Prestin).
source: Their conservation within the SLC26 family is illustrated in the comparison of the respective domains of SLC26A6 and SLC26A5 (Prestin; Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C, D, E, G).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: SLC26A5 belongs to a protein that confers electromotility instead of transporting ions.
source: Latter belongs to a protein that, instead of transporting ions, confers electromotility and which in the best defined structure (PDBID: 7LGU) resides in a distinct conformation where the substrate binding site has become buried between core and gate domain (leading to an RMSD of 2.9 Å for the entire TMD; Ge et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Despite the functional and conformational differences, the core domains of SLC26A5 and SLC26A6 superimpose with an RMSD of only 1.13 Å, illustrating their close structural resemblance.
source: Despite the functional and conformational differences, the core domains of SLC26A5 and SLC26A6 superimpose with an RMSD of only 1.13 Å, illustrating their close structural resemblance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C.

claim: SLC26A6 and SLC26A5 share similar ion binding properties that extend to Cl- and HCO3-, latter of which is not a substrate of SLC26A9.
source: Both proteins share similar ion binding properties that extends to Cl- and HCO3-, latter of which is not a substrate of SLC26A9 (Walter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and the current structural data.

claim: The comparison of the core domains of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 shows distinct features that likely underlie the differences in substrate selectivity and transport mechanism.
source: In contrast to the general similarity with SLC26A5, the comparison of the same units of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 shows distinct features that likely underlie the differences in substrate selectivity and transport mechanism (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: The differences between SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 core domains are confined to the conformation of α10, which at its N-terminus forms direct interactions with transported ions, whereas the remainder of the domain is very similar.
source: These are confined to the conformation of α10, which at its N-terminus forms direct interactions with transported ions, whereas the remainder of the domain is very similar (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: The difference in the conformations of α10 between SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 can be approximated by a 12–14° rotation of α10 of SLC26A9 around an axis located at its C-terminal end towards α-helix 1.
source: The difference in the conformations of this short membrane-inserted helix can be approximated by a 12–14° rotation of α10 of SLC26A9 around an axis located at its C-terminal end towards α-helix 1 (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: The replacement of residues within the contact region of SLC26A9 in comparison to other family members acts to lower their side chain volume at the contact region between α1 and α10.
source: The replacement of residues within the contact region of SLC26A9 in comparison to other family members acts to lower their side chain volume at the contact region between both helices (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4C–F.

claim: Ser 96 and Val 100 on SLC26A6 are both replaced by glycines at equivalent positions in SLC26A9 (i.e., Gly 77 and Gly 81).
source: These include Ser 96 and Val 100 on SLC26A6, which are both replaced by glycines at equivalent positions in SLC26A9 (i.e., Gly 77 and Gly 81) and a substitution of Val 407, Gln 408 and Thr 411 by Ala 396, Val 397 and Ala 400 (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4C–F.

claim: Val 407, Gln 408 and Thr 411 in SLC26A6 are substituted by Ala 396, Val 397 and Ala 400 in SLC26A9.
source: These include Ser 96 and Val 100 on SLC26A6, which are both replaced by glycines at equivalent positions in SLC26A9 (i.e., Gly 77 and Gly 81) and a substitution of Val 407, Gln 408 and Thr 411 by Ala 396, Val 397 and Ala 400 (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4C–F.

claim: There are differences in the side chains surrounding the ion binding site between SLC26A6 and SLC26A9, which together determine the size and polarity of the substrate binding pocket.
source: In addition to the described substitutions, there are also differences in the side chains surrounding the ion binding site, which together determine the size and polarity of the substrate binding pocket (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Ser 401 of SLC26A6 is replaced by an alanine in SLC26A9 (Ala 390).
source: These differences extend to Ser 401 of SLC26A6, which is replaced by an alanine in SLC26A9 (Ala 390), and most prominent, the large Arg 404 of SLC26A6, which is replaced by Val 393 in SLC26A9 (Figure 4C-I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4C-I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G.

claim: The large Arg 404 of SLC26A6 is replaced by Val 393 in SLC26A9.
source: These differences extend to Ser 401 of SLC26A6, which is replaced by an alanine in SLC26A9 (Ala 390), and most prominent, the large Arg 404 of SLC26A6, which is replaced by Val 393 in SLC26A9 (Figure 4C-I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4C-I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G.

claim: The pocket is considerably deeper in SLC26A9 compared to SLC26A6, where it is delimited by the side chain of Arg 404 that interacts with the residues preceding α helix 3 to form the back side of the shallow binding site.
source: As a result, the pocket is considerably deeper in SLC26A9 compared SLC26A6, where it is delimited by the side chain of Arg 404 that interacts with the residues preceding α helix 3 to form the back side of the shallow binding site (Figure 4D–I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–H).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4D–I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–H.

claim: Arg 404 likely contributes to the stabilization of bound anions by coulombic interactions, with its guanidium group potentially engaging in direct interactions with bicarbonate or oxalate.
source: In addition to its structural role, Arg 404 likely also contributes to the stabilization of bound anions by coulombic interactions, with its guanidium group potentially engaging in direct interactions with bicarbonate or oxalate.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observation and chemical properties of arginine.

claim: The altered geometry of the binding site leads to the binding of Cl- deeper in the pocket in case of SLC26A9.
source: The altered geometry of the site leads to the binding of Cl- deeper in the pocket in case of SLC26A9 (Figure 4D, E,G-I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H) and presumably explains why bicarbonate interacts with SLC26A6 but not SLC26A9.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4D, E, G-I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The altered geometry of the binding site presumably explains why bicarbonate interacts with SLC26A6 but not SLC26A9.
source: The altered geometry of the site leads to the binding of Cl- deeper in the pocket in case of SLC26A9 (Figure 4D, E,G-I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H) and presumably explains why bicarbonate interacts with SLC26A6 but not SLC26A9.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural differences.

claim: The mutation R404V in SLC26A6 is well-tolerated and does not interfere with protein integrity as judged by its expression level and biochemical properties.
source: This mutation is well-tolerated and does not interfere with protein integrity as judged by its expression level and biochemical properties.
evidence: This is supported by the functional data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Small currents were detected for SLC26A6 R404V in whole-cell patch clamp experiments in symmetric Cl- solutions, which are low compared to SLC26A9.
source: In whole-cell patch clamp experiments, we detected small currents in symmetric Cl- solutions, which are low compared to SLC26A9, despite the comparable expression of the mutant at the cell-surface (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B–E.

claim: The currents detected for SLC26A6 R404V are not significantly higher than SLC26A6 WT.
source: Irrespective of their magnitude, which is not significantly higher than SLC26A6 WT (Figure 5C and D), these currents are indicative for the capability of the mutant to mediate electrogenic Cl- transport at low rates.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The currents detected for SLC26A6 R404V are indicative for the capability of the mutant to mediate electrogenic Cl- transport at low rates.
source: Irrespective of their magnitude, which is not significantly higher than SLC26A6 WT (Figure 5C and D), these currents are indicative for the capability of the mutant to mediate electrogenic Cl- transport at low rates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiology data.

claim: The proteoliposome-based ACMA assay confirmed that the R404V mutation has conferred the ability to SLC26A6 to pass downhill Cl- transport.
source: We thus turned to our proteoliposome-based ACMA assay to confirm that side chain replacement has indeed conferred the ability to SLC26A6 to pass downhill Cl- transport (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The mutant SLC26A6 R404V did not show pronounced Cl- flux in the lucigenin assay for coupled Cl-/HCO3- exchange.
source: After demonstrating uncoupled chloride transport, we tested whether the mutant has retained its ability of mediating coupled Cl-/HCO3- exchange using the fluorophore lucigenin but did not find pronounced Cl- flux in this case (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: The mutation of a conserved basic position in the ion binding site has compromised the ability of SLC26A6 to mediate coupled Cl-/HCO3- exchange and instead facilitated uncoupled Cl- transport with slow kinetics.
source: Together our data suggest that the mutation of a conserved basic position in the ion binding site has compromised the ability of SLC26A6 to mediate coupled Cl-/HCO3- exchange and instead facilitated uncoupled Cl- transport with slow kinetics.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The mutation of a single residue is insufficient to confer the complete functional phenotype of SLC26A9 as a fast uncoupled Cl- conductor.
source: While these findings underline the importance of Arg 404 for anion interactions and coupling, they also emphasize that the mutation of a single residue is insufficient to confer the complete functional phenotype of SLC26A9 as a fast uncoupled Cl- conductor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data of the R404V mutant.

claim: The results underline the importance of the anion binding site in SLC26 transporters for the transport mechanism of its members.
source: Nevertheless, our results further underline the importance of the anion binding site in SLC26 transporters for the transport mechanism of its members.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and functional data.

claim: SLC26A6 mediates electroneutral Cl-/HCO3- exchange.
source: The protein mediates electroneutral Cl-/ HCO3- and presumable electrogenic Cl-/oxalate exchange, which is in stark contrast to the uncoupled Cl- transport of SLC26A9.
evidence: This is supported by the functional data presented in Figure 1.

claim: SLC26A6 mediates presumable electrogenic Cl-/oxalate exchange.
source: The protein mediates electroneutral Cl-/ HCO3- and presumable electrogenic Cl-/oxalate exchange, which is in stark contrast to the uncoupled Cl- transport of SLC26A9.
evidence: This is supported by the functional data presented in Figure 1H.

claim: The altered ion binding site in SLC26A6 is located in the mobile core domain of the transmembrane transport unit.
source: This is accomplished by an altered ion binding site located in the mobile core domain of the transmembrane transport unit.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In the case of Cl-/HCO3- transport by SLC26A6, there is a strict equimolar exchange of anions binding to a conserved site in the mobile core domain of the transmembrane transport unit.
source: In the case of Cl-/HCO3- transport, we detect a strict equimolar exchange of anions binding to a conserved site in the mobile core domain of the transmembrane transport unit (Figure 4B and H).
evidence: This is supported by the functional and structural data presented in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: An analogous mechanism is assumed for Cl-/oxalate exchange by SLC26A6.
source: Although not shown unambiguously, we assume an analogous mechanism also for Cl-/oxalate exchange.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the functional data.

claim: Transport by SLC26A6 would be electroneutral in case of the monovalent HCO3- and electrogenic in case of the divalent oxalate.
source: Consequently, transport would be electroneutral in case of the monovalent HCO3- and electrogenic in case of the divalent oxalate (Figure 1E–H), which was already proposed in a previous study (Chernova et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the functional data and citation to prior work.

claim: SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 show different features with respect to substrate selectivity and coupling.
source: Regarding their function, SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 show different features with respect to substrate selectivity and coupling (Ohana et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the functional data and citation to prior work.

claim: Both SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 are capable of interacting with Cl- with similar mM affinity.
source: Remarkably, both proteins are capable of interacting with Cl- with similar mM affinity (Figure 1F; Walter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the functional data shown in Figure 1F and citation to prior work.

claim: SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 interact with Cl- via distinct interactions in equivalent binding regions.
source: However, they do this via distinct interactions in equivalent binding regions.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 4.

claim: In SLC26A9, Cl- binds in a deep pocket with low field strength.
source: In SLC26A9, Cl- binds in a deep pocket with low field strength, whereas the same pocket is shallower in SLC26A6, where a conserved arginine (Arg 404) increases the positive electrostatic potential and thus likely stabilizes the bound anion (Figure 4H, I and Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4H, I and Figure 6.

claim: In SLC26A6, the Cl- binding pocket is shallower, where a conserved arginine (Arg 404) increases the positive electrostatic potential and thus likely stabilizes the bound anion.
source: In SLC26A9, Cl- binds in a deep pocket with low field strength, whereas the same pocket is shallower in SLC26A6, where a conserved arginine (Arg 404) increases the positive electrostatic potential and thus likely stabilizes the bound anion (Figure 4H, I and Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4H, I and Figure 6.

claim: Together with the presence of additional residues at the binding site (i.e., Ser 401 at the N-terminal end of α10), the captured Cl- in SLC26A6 can rely on a larger density of polar interactions.
source: Together with the presence of additional residues at the binding site (i.e., Ser 401 at the N-terminal end of α10), the captured Cl- in SLC26A6 thus can rely on a larger density of polar interactions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: The binding site in SLC26A6 likely provides a suitable environment for HCO3- and oxalate, neither of which are substrates of SLC26A9.
source: The same site likely also provides a suitable environment for HCO3- and oxalate, neither of which are substrates of SLC26A9 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,H; Dorwart et al., 2007; Walter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and functional properties.

claim: A similar anion interaction observed in SLC26A6 is also found in the paralogs SLC26A4 (Pendrin) and SLC26A5 (Prestin), which both share a similar substrate preference.
source: A similar anion interaction observed in SLC26A6 is also found in the paralogs SLC26A4 (Pendrin) (Liu et al., 2023) and SLC26A5 (Prestin) (Futamata et al., 2022; Ge et al., 2021), which both share a similar substrate preference.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: The similarity between the core domains of SLC26A6 and Prestin is remarkable in light of the altered function of Prestin, which is no longer capable of transporting ions and instead operates as motor protein in cochlear outer hair cells of mammals.
source: The similarity between the core domains of SLC26A6 and Prestin is remarkable in light of the altered function of the latter, which is no longer capable of transporting ions and instead operates as motor protein in cochlear outer hair cells of mammals (Zheng et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Prestin undergoes comparable conformational changes as other family members to some degree, as illustrated in the close relationship between occluded conformations of SLC26A9 and SLC26A5.
source: While to some degree Prestin undergoes comparable conformational changes as other family members, as illustrated in the close relationship between occluded conformations of SLC26A9 and SLC26A5, the full transition into an outward-facing conformation to release the bound anion to the extracellular environment appears to be prohibited (Bavi et al., 2021; Ge et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: The full transition of Prestin into an outward-facing conformation to release the bound anion to the extracellular environment appears to be prohibited.
source: While to some degree Prestin undergoes comparable conformational changes as other family members, as illustrated in the close relationship between occluded conformations of SLC26A9 and SLC26A5, the full transition into an outward-facing conformation to release the bound anion to the extracellular environment appears to be prohibited (Bavi et al., 2021; Ge et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: SLC26A9 and SLC26A6 are distinguished by the sequence of conformations that together define the transport cycle.
source: From a mechanistic viewpoint SLC26A9 and SLC26A6 are distinguished by the sequence of conformations that together define the transport cycle (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and functional data.

claim: In the uncoupled SLC26A9, the transporter is able to transition between inward- and outward facing states at a high rate, which underlies the pronounced currents observed in patch clamp experiments.
source: In the uncoupled SLC26A9, the transporter is able to transition between inward- and outward facing states at a high rate, which underlies the pronounced currents observed in patch clamp experiments (Figure 6B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data.

claim: The change of access in an unloaded conformation is kinetically unfavorable in the coupled exchanger SLC26A6, as illustrated in the lack of current in electrophysiological recordings and the absence of a Cl- leak in a vesicle-based assay.
source: The same change of the access in an unloaded conformation is kinetically unfavorable in the coupled exchanger SLC26A6, as illustrated in the lack of current in electrophysiological recordings and the absence of a Cl- leak in a vesicle-based assay (Figures 1B–D ,–6A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data.

claim: The basis for the distinctive kinetic features of SLC26A9 and SLC26A6 is currently still unclear.
source: The basis for the distinctive kinetic features of both paralogs is currently still unclear, and we do at this stage not exclude the existence of a leaky channel-like conformation in SLC26A9.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in the current understanding.

claim: The existence of a leaky channel-like conformation in SLC26A9 is not excluded, which could potentially promote Cl- flow across a continuous aqueous pore without obligatory protein movement, although there is currently no structural evidence for its existence.
source: The basis for the distinctive kinetic features of both paralogs is currently still unclear, and we do at this stage not exclude the existence of a leaky channel-like conformation in SLC26A9. Such a conformation could potentially promote Cl- flow across a continuous aqueous pore without obligatory protein movement, although there is currently no structural evidence for its existence.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: The nature of the energy barrier, which prevents the shuttling of the unloaded state of SLC26A6 and other paralogs with similar functional phenotype, has thus far remained elusive.
source: The nature of the energy barrier, which prevents the shuttling of the unloaded state of SLC26A6 and other paralogs with similar functional phenotype (i.e. the transporters SLC26A1-4) has thus far remained elusive.
evidence: This acknowledges a knowledge gap.

claim: Conformational changes in SLC26 transporters are likely dictated by interactions between the mobile core domain with the immobile gate domain, which are both believed to operate as semi-independent entities.
source: It is likely that conformational changes are dictated by interactions between the mobile core domain with the immobile gate domain, which are both believed to operate as semi-independent entities (Geertsma et al., 2015; Walter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural knowledge and citations to prior work.

claim: Both core and gate domains bury a similar contact area in the inward-facing conformations of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 and do not exhibit pronounced differences in their interactions.
source: Remarkably, both units bury a similar contact area in the inward-facing conformations of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9 and do not exhibit pronounced differences in their interactions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Additional contacts in SLC26A6 are established with the structured N-terminal part of the IVS region of the STAS domain of the interacting subunit, which appear to further stabilize the observed inward-facing conformation.
source: Additional contacts in SLC26A6 are established with the structured N-terminal part of the IVS region of the STAS domain of the interacting subunit, which appear to further stabilize the observed inward-facing conformation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Similar interactions between the IVS and the core domain have also been found in the full-length transporter SLC26A9.
source: Similar interactions have also been found in the full-length transporter SLC26A9 (Chi et al., 2020), which, next to the increased surface expression, could account for the strongly increased activity observed in the construct SLC26A9T where the IVS sequence of the protein was removed (Walter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The truncation of the C-terminus of SLC26A9 might have contributed to the high activity observed in the construct SLC26A9T.
source: Besides the effect of the IVS, also the truncation of the C-terminus of SLC26A9 might have contributed to this high activity.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible contributing factor.

claim: The unstructured C-termini of SLC26 family members are weakly conserved and in case of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9, they contain a PDZ binding motif at their end.
source: The unstructured C-termini of family members are weakly conserved and in case of SLC26A6 and SLC26A9, they contain a PDZ binding motif at their end, which is believed to tether either transporter to potential partners such as the anion channel CFTR via interacting scaffolding proteins (Shcheynikov et al., 2006a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the isoform b of SLC26A9, a C-terminal extension was located in the aqueous cavity leading to the substrate binding site in the inward-facing conformation of SLC26A9, thereby locking the transporter in the observed conformation.
source: In the isoform b of SLC26A9, a C-terminal extension was located in the aqueous cavity leading to the substrate binding site in the inward-facing conformation of SLC26A9, thereby locking the transporter in the observed conformation (Chi et al., 2020; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: There is no similar C-terminal extension found in any SLC26A6 isoforms.
source: There is no similar extension found in any SLC26A6 isoforms, and the role of this interaction in a cellular environment is currently unclear, although it hints at a possible regulation in SLC26A9.
evidence: This is an observation based on sequence analysis.

claim: The role of the C-terminal extension interaction in SLC26A9 in a cellular environment is currently unclear, although it hints at a possible regulation.
source: There is no similar extension found in any SLC26A6 isoforms, and the role of this interaction in a cellular environment is currently unclear, although it hints at a possible regulation in SLC26A9.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible regulatory mechanism.

claim: The study has provided novel insight into the structural basis of substrate selectivity and the mechanistic distinction between uncoupled and coupled transporters of the SLC26 family.
source: Collectively, our study has provided novel insight into the structural basis of substrate selectivity and the mechanistic distinction between uncoupled and coupled transporters of the SLC26 family and thus provides a foundation for future investigations.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's contributions.
